Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The government is warning that taking the psoriasis drug Raptiva could result in serious brain infection and even death. Raptiva may cause a serious brain infection called progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The Food and Drug Administration cited three confirmed cases, and a possible fourth, of people diagnosed with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) after being treated with Raptiva. "Three of those patients have died," the FDA said in a public health advisory. "All four patients were treated with the drug for more than three years." None was receiving other treatments that suppress the immune system. Raptiva's product labeling was revised in October to highlight a boxed warning about the risks of life-threatening infections, including PML. "At that time, the FDA directed Genentech, the manufacturer, to develop a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) to include a medication guide to educate patients about the drug's risks," the FDA's advisory says. In the advisory, issued Thursday, the FDA highlighted the confirmed cases and promised to "take appropriate steps" to ensure that Raptiva's risks do not outweigh its benefits. The FDA also said it will ensure that patients "are clearly informed of the signs and symptoms of PML" and that health care professionals "carefully monitor patients for the possible development of PML." Overseas, the European Medicines Agency has gone further, recommending that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued and that patients taking the drug talk to their doctors about an alternative. On Thursday it asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally binding. The group's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use determined "that the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks, because of safety concerns, including the occurrence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in patients taking the medicine." It said patients who have been treated with the drug should be "closely monitored for neurological symptoms and symptoms of infection." "Patients who are currently taking Raptiva should not stop treatment abruptly, but should make an appointment with their doctor to discuss the most appropriate replacement treatment," the agency said. Raptiva, a once-weekly injection for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, works by suppressing T-cells -- cells that help fight infection -- in the immune system. Those cells cause the skin inflammation associated with psoriasis. By suppressing T-cells, Raptiva "decreases the function of the immune system, which increases a patient's susceptibility to infections," the FDA said. The National Institutes of Health says the prognosis for PML "remains grim; the disease usually lasts for months and 80 percent die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been reported. Those who survive PML can be left with severe neurological disabilities." Around 6 million to 7 million Americans have psoriasis, which is incurable, the NIH says.

# Government Health Officials Alert Public to Dangerous Side Effects of Psoriasis Medication

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Federal health authorities have issued a warning that Raptiva, a medication prescribed for psoriasis, carries the risk of triggering a potentially fatal brain infection. The condition in question, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), has been confirmed in three patients who took the drug, with a fourth case suspected, according to the Food and Drug Administration.

Of these four documented cases, three individuals have since passed away, the FDA disclosed in a health advisory released to the public. Notably, all four patients had been undergoing Raptiva treatment for a period exceeding three years, and none were simultaneously receiving other immune-suppressing therapies.

This past October, the drug's official labeling underwent revision to include a prominent boxed warning highlighting the dangers of severe infections like PML. According to the FDA's advisory statement, regulators had instructed Genentech—the company that manufactures Raptiva—to establish a comprehensive risk evaluation and mitigation strategy, which would include distributing educational materials to help patients understand the medication's potential dangers.

In Thursday's advisory, the agency drew attention to the confirmed PML cases and pledged to implement measures ensuring the drug's benefits continue to justify its risks. Additionally, the FDA committed to guaranteeing that patients receive clear information regarding warning signs of PML, while urging physicians to closely watch their patients for any indications that the condition might be developing.

European regulators have taken a more aggressive stance on the matter. The European Medicines Agency advised against writing any new prescriptions for Raptiva, urging existing patients to consult with their physicians about switching to alternative treatments. The agency escalated this recommendation on Thursday by petitioning the European Commission to transform it into binding legal policy.

The agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use concluded that the drug's risks—particularly the emergence of PML among users—now outweigh whatever therapeutic benefits it provides. The committee advised that patients previously treated with Raptiva undergo careful observation for neurological or infection-related symptoms. Furthermore, the agency cautioned against patients abruptly discontinuing the medication on their own, instead recommending they schedule consultations with their doctors to identify suitable alternative treatments.

Administered as a weekly injection, Raptiva is designed for adults dealing with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. The drug functions by dampening the activity of T-cells—immune system components that normally combat infection but also contribute to the skin inflammation characteristic of psoriasis. This suppression of T-cell activity, the FDA explained, weakens overall immune function and leaves patients more vulnerable to infections.

According to the National Institutes of Health, the outlook for those diagnosed with PML remains bleak. The illness typically progresses over several months, claiming the lives of roughly 80 percent of patients within the first half-year, though some cases of unexpected recovery have been documented. Survivors frequently face lasting and severe neurological impairments.

Psoriasis itself affects approximately 6 to 7 million people across the United States and currently has no cure, according to NIH data.

# FDA Issues Warning on Raptiva Over Rare Brain Infection Risk

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has issued a significant safety warning regarding Raptiva (efalizumab), a medication used to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, citing concerns that the drug may increase the risk of a rare but serious neurological condition known as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). This brain infection, which attacks the central nervous system, can lead to severe disability or death, and currently has no effective treatment or cure.

## Documented Cases Raise Alarm

The FDA's warning stems from an analysis of confirmed and suspected cases linked to Raptiva use. Regulators identified three confirmed cases of PML in patients undergoing treatment with the drug, along with a fourth case that remains under investigation as a probable instance of the disease. Tragically, three of these patients died after being on Raptiva therapy for more than three years, underscoring the potential long-term risks associated with extended use of the medication.

## Regulatory Response and Labeling Changes

In response to these findings, the FDA took action in October by mandating a revision to Raptiva's product labeling. The updated label now includes a boxed warning—the agency's most serious form of caution—specifically highlighting the risk of PML. Additionally, the FDA has directed Genentech, the drug's manufacturer, to develop and implement a comprehensive risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS). This strategy includes the creation of a patient medication guide designed to ensure that individuals prescribed Raptiva are fully informed of the potential dangers before beginning treatment.

## Ongoing Monitoring and Commitment to Safety

The FDA has committed to continuously evaluating the risk-benefit profile of Raptiva as new data becomes available. The agency emphasized its responsibility to keep both patients and healthcare providers well-informed about the warning signs and symptoms of PML, as well as the importance of regular monitoring throughout the course of treatment. This ongoing vigilance is intended to help catch potential cases early and minimize adverse outcomes for patients who continue to use the medication under medical supervision.

## A Stronger Stance from European Regulators

While the FDA opted for enhanced warnings and monitoring protocols, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has taken a notably more cautious and assertive approach. The EMA has recommended that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued, effectively calling for a halt to new patient starts on the drug. Furthermore, the agency has urged patients currently undergoing treatment with Raptiva to consult with their healthcare providers about transitioning to alternative therapies.

Beyond these recommendations, the EMA is pursuing measures to strengthen the enforceability of its guidance. The agency is working through the European Commission to make its recommendation legally binding across European Union member states, a move that would give the warning significant regulatory weight and compel stricter compliance from prescribers and manufacturers alike. This divergence in regulatory strategy between the FDA and EMA highlights differing approaches to balancing patient access to treatment against the imperative of minimizing serious health risks.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued a public health advisory regarding Raptiva (efalizumab), a biologic medication used to treat chronic plaque psoriasis, after reports linked the drug to a rare and often fatal brain infection.

## The Safety Concern

The FDA's advisory centered on cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a serious brain infection caused by the reactivation of the JC virus in immunocompromised patients. PML has no known cure and frequently results in severe disability or death. Because Raptiva works by suppressing the immune system to treat psoriasis, patients taking the drug face reduced defenses against opportunistic infections like the one responsible for PML.

## Regulatory Response

**In Europe:** Regulatory authorities moved swiftly, with the European Medicines Agency recommending the suspension of Raptiva's marketing authorization. This effectively pulled the drug from the European market pending further safety review.

**In the United States:** The FDA's response was initially more measured, opting to issue a public health advisory to alert physicians and patients to the risk rather than immediately withdrawing the drug from the market. The advisory urged healthcare providers to monitor patients for neurological symptoms that could indicate PML and to discontinue treatment if such signs appeared.

## Context and Implications

The divergent regulatory approaches—outright suspension in Europe versus a cautionary advisory in the U.S.—highlighted differing risk-tolerance frameworks between regulatory bodies handling the same safety signal. The case ultimately became a significant example in discussions about post-market drug surveillance, particularly for immunosuppressive biologics, and the challenges regulators face in balancing patient access to treatment against emerging safety risks discovered after a drug reaches the market.

# Efalizumab (Raptiva) Withdrawn Amid PML Risk Concerns

**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**

Regulatory health agencies in the United States and Europe have taken decisive action against Raptiva (efalizumab), a biologic drug used to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, after new evidence linked the medication to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a rare but frequently fatal brain infection.

## What is Happening

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) have both issued statements addressing safety concerns surrounding efalizumab, a monoclonal antibody that works by suppressing certain immune system functions to reduce psoriasis symptoms.

## The FDA's Position

According to FDA safety communications, the agency identified multiple confirmed cases of PML in patients receiving long-term efalizumab therapy. The FDA noted that the drug's mechanism of action—which involves inhibiting T-cell activity to control the autoimmune response driving psoriasis—may leave patients vulnerable to reactivation of the JC virus, the pathogen responsible for causing PML in immunocompromised individuals.

The FDA emphasized that the majority of affected patients had been on the drug for three years or longer, suggesting a cumulative risk associated with prolonged immunosuppression. The agency has classified PML as a rare but serious adverse event warranting market withdrawal rather than a simple label update, given the severity and often irreversible nature of the condition.

## The EMA's Assessment

The European Medicines Agency conducted a parallel review and reached similar conclusions. In its official statement, the EMA indicated that the risk-benefit profile of efalizumab had shifted unfavorably, citing the same pattern of PML cases reported to European pharmacovigilance databases.

The EMA's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) reportedly recommended suspension of the drug's marketing authorization, concluding that the risk of a potentially fatal brain infection outweighed the benefits of treating a non-life-threatening skin condition when alternative psoriasis therapies remain available.

## Understanding PML

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a serious viral infection of the brain caused by the JC virus, which lies dormant in most healthy adults but can become active and cause severe neurological damage when the immune system is significantly suppressed. Symptoms include progressive weakness, vision problems, cognitive decline, and difficulty with coordination. There is no cure for PML, and the condition is fatal in a substantial percentage of cases.

## What This Means for Patients

Both regulatory bodies have urged physicians to:

- Discontinue efalizumab treatment in current patients
- Monitor patients who have recently stopped the drug for neurological symptoms
- Consider alternative psoriasis treatments with established safety profiles
- Report any suspicious neurological symptoms immediately

Patients currently taking Raptiva are advised to consult their healthcare providers promptly rather than discontinuing treatment abruptly without medical guidance, as sudden withdrawal from immunosuppressive therapy can carry its own risks.

## Industry Response

The manufacturer has been in communication with both regulatory agencies throughout the review process. Market withdrawal procedures are expected to follow standard regulatory protocols in both jurisdictions.

---

*This report reflects publicly available regulatory communications. Patients with questions about their treatment should consult their prescribing physician or dermatologist.*

# FDA Warns of Serious Brain Infection Risk Linked to Psoriasis Drug Raptiva

## Regulatory Alert Highlights Rare but Fatal Neurological Complication

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has issued a safety warning regarding Raptiva (efalizumab), a biologic medication used to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, citing an elevated risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a rare but frequently fatal brain infection.

The FDA's announcement comes after the agency identified confirmed and suspected cases of PML in patients receiving long-term treatment with Raptiva, manufactured by Genentech. The warning underscores growing concerns about immunosuppressive therapies and their potential to unmask latent viral infections in the central nervous system.

## Understanding Psoriasis and Its Treatment

Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune skin condition affecting millions of Americans, characterized by red, scaly patches that result from the rapid overproduction of skin cells. The condition ranges from mild, localized patches to severe cases covering large portions of the body, significantly impacting patients' quality of life.

For moderate-to-severe cases that don't respond to topical treatments, physicians often turn to systemic therapies, including biologic drugs like Raptiva. Approved by the FDA in 2003, Raptiva works by suppressing specific immune system functions—specifically T-cell activation—to reduce the inflammatory response responsible for psoriasis symptoms.

While effective for many patients, this immunosuppressive mechanism carries inherent risks, as it can compromise the body's ability to fight off certain infections and control latent viruses.

## What Is PML?

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a rare but severe brain infection caused by the JC virus, a common polyomavirus that most people are exposed to during childhood without ever developing symptoms. In individuals with healthy immune systems, the virus typically remains dormant and harmless.

However, when the immune system is significantly weakened—whether through disease, chemotherapy, or immunosuppressive medications—the JC virus can reactivate and attack the brain's white matter, leading to progressive and irreversible neurological damage.

PML symptoms often develop gradually and may include:

- Clumsiness or loss of coordination
- Progressive weakness on one side of the body
- Vision problems
- Changes in personality, memory, or cognitive function
- Difficulty speaking

## A Grim Prognosis

The prognosis for patients diagnosed with PML remains poor. According to medical literature, the condition carries a mortality rate that historically ranged from 30 to 50 percent within the first few months of diagnosis, with many survivors experiencing significant, permanent neurological disability.

There is no cure for PML, and treatment primarily focuses on restoring immune function—typically by discontinuing the immunosuppressive therapy responsible for the reactivation—in hopes that the body's own defenses can eventually control the virus. However, by the time symptoms become apparent, substantial and often irreversible brain damage may have already occurred.

This grim outlook has made PML a significant concern for regulators monitoring biologic and immunosuppressive drugs, particularly following similar warnings issued for other medications, including natalizumab (Tysabri), used to treat multiple sclerosis and Crohn's disease.

## FDA's Response and Recommendations

In light of the reported PML cases associated with Raptiva, the FDA has strengthened warning labels and is urging healthcare providers to:

- Carefully weigh the risks and benefits before prescribing Raptiva, particularly for long-term use
- Monitor patients closely for any new neurological symptoms
- Discontinue treatment immediately if PML is suspected
- Refer patients exhibiting suspicious symptoms for prompt neurological evaluation, including MRI imaging and JC virus testing when appropriate

The agency has also required Genentech to include more prominent warnings in the drug's labeling, ensuring both physicians and patients are fully informed of the potential risks before beginning or continuing treatment.

## Broader Implications for Biologic Therapies

This warning adds to a growing body of evidence linking certain immunosuppressive biologic drugs to PML, prompting increased scrutiny across the pharmaceutical industry. Physicians are increasingly encouraged to conduct thorough risk assessments before initiating these therapies and to maintain vigilant, ongoing monitoring throughout treatment.

Patients currently using Raptiva are advised not to discontinue the medication without consulting their healthcare provider, as abrupt cessation can trigger other complications. Instead, they should discuss any concerns and watch for warning signs, seeking immediate medical attention if new neurological symptoms arise.

The FDA has indicated it will continue to monitor safety data and may issue further updates as more information becomes available.
